content: The term red eye refers to a common ophthalmologic condition frequently encountered in pediatric primary care settings. It can result from inflammation in various parts of the eye, including the lacrimal glands, eyelids, or due to an abnormal tear film. Primary care physicians often manage red eye effectively, but recognizing when to refer patients to an ophthalmologist is critical. Baseline ophthalmologic tests and associated symptoms can help narrow the differential diagnosis. Key factors such as the duration of symptoms, whether they are unilateral or bilateral, and the severity of pain are essential in distinguishing between non-critical conditions manageable by a general practitioner, conditions requiring elective referral to an ophthalmologist, and true ocular emergencies necessitating urgent surgical intervention. Causes of Red Eye Life-Threatening Causes Life-threatening causes of red eye include conditions that, if untreated, could result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours. These include: Globe ruptures or perforations Intraocular infections Carotid-cavernous sinus fistula Common Causes Infectious Causes Bacterial conjunctivitis Viral conjunctivitis Iritis/iridocyclitis Anterior uveitis Posterior uveitis (choroiditis) Endophthalmitis Dacryocystitis Non-Infectious Causes Acute angle-closure glaucoma Disorders of the ocular adnexa (e.g., hordeolum, eyelid malposition) Scleritis/episcleritis Photokeratitis Corneal erosion or ulceration Subconjunctival hemorrhage Allergic conjunctivitis Non-infectious (kerato)conjunctivitis Contact lens-related issues Blunt or penetrating trauma Foreign bodies Chemical conjunctivitis Blepharitis Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE) Patients presenting with red eye are commonly seen in pediatric primary care clinics. Although the differential diagnosis is broad, a concise history and physical examination can often lead to a definitive diagnosis. Identifying vision-threatening conditions and understanding the urgency of referral to an ophthalmologist are paramount. Certain systemic diseases, such as leukemia, sarcoidosis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis, may also present with red eye as a primary symptom. Diagnostic Approach Red eye in pediatric patients can be categorized into localized, diffuse, and perilimbal (perikeratic) injection patterns. Diagnostic algorithms, such as those outlined in the Nelson Essentials of Pediatrics, can guide clinicians in identifying the underlying cause. Treatment Treatment strategies for red eye are summarized in guidelines such as those from the American Journal of Medicine: Good hygiene practices, including meticulous handwashing, are essential to reduce the spread of acute viral conjunctivitis. Any ophthalmic antibiotic may be used for acute bacterial conjunctivitis, as they generally have similar cure rates. Mild allergic conjunctivitis can be managed with over-the-counter antihistamine/vasoconstrictor agents or more effective second-generation topical histamine H1 receptor antagonists. Moderate dry eye may benefit from therapies such as topical cyclosporine, topical corticosteroids, and systemic omega-3 fatty acids. Patients with chronic blepharitis unresponsive to eyelid hygiene and topical antibiotics may require oral tetracycline or doxycycline. Do's The primary goal is to identify potentially serious ocular conditions and ensure immediate referral to an ophthalmologist for appropriate treatment. Conditions requiring referral include orbital cellulitis, hyphema, scleritis, iritis or uveitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and corneal abrasions (unless very superficial). Exercise caution when prescribing steroids; herpetic keratitis must be ruled out. Ocular pain and changes in vision are critical warning signs of serious eye pathology. Unless a benign diagnosis is certain, patients with these symptoms should be referred for ophthalmologic assessment. Don'ts Do not overlook the pupillary exam in pediatric patients, as it is a vital component of the clinical workup. Pupillary abnormalities, such as anisocoria, light-near dissociation, afferent pupillary defects, or paradoxical pupillary constriction in the dark, can serve as red flags necessitating further evaluation. Through careful physical examination, detailed history-taking, and observation, clinicians can detect potentially visionand life-threatening conditions.
